title: Remote control, signal limits and foreign operation
blurb: Know the control-link, spurious and modulation limits, the 630 m and 2200 m notification, and the CEPT and IARP arrangements.

E1C01.why: Data on 60 m is limited to **2.8 kHz** bandwidth, which fits inside a channel.

E1C02.why: To foreign amateurs, keep to matters **incidental to amateur radio and personal remarks**. English is not required.
E1C02.trap: Third-party limits and English-only are not what the rule says.

E1C03.why: After **30 days** you may operate, unless told you are within **1 km** of PLC systems on those frequencies. No approval is required.

E1C04.why: An IARP is a permit that lets US amateurs operate in **certain countries of the Americas**.

E1C05.why: An automatically controlled station may carry third-party traffic **only in RTTY or data emissions**.
E1C05.trap: Voice and CW are not allowed for automatic third-party traffic.

E1C06.why: CEPT operation requires a copy of **FCC Public Notice DA 16-1048**. No "/CEPT" suffix or local-language ID.

E1C07.why: Inform the **Utilities Technology Council** of your **call sign and station coordinates**. No FCC endorsement.

E1C08.why: If the control link fails, a remotely controlled station may transmit for at most **3 minutes**.

E1C09.why: Below 29.0 MHz, angle modulation may not exceed a modulation index of **1.0** at the highest modulating frequency.

E1C10.why: Spurious emissions below 30 MHz must be **-43 dB** relative to the fundamental. Bigger negative means weaker.
E1C10.trap: -53 dB and beyond are stricter than the actual limit.

E1C11.why: **CEPT** is the arrangement that lets US amateurs operate in many European countries and vice versa.
E1C11.trap: IARP covers the Americas; "ITU reciprocal license" is not the answer.

E1C12.why: Phone emissions are permitted on the **entire** 630 m band.
